title: The Emperor's Milk Reservoir and the Shared Blame (HI)
summary: Akbar tests his citizens' civic honesty by ordering each household to contribute a cup of milk to a dark pool. Morning reveals a reservoir of water.
full_text:
During an evening assembly at Fatehpur Sikri, Emperor Akbar praised the selfless devotion of his citizens, claiming that every family in Agra would gladly sacrifice their finest goods for the prosperity of the realm.

Birbal remarked quietly: 'Sire, people are generous when their names are proclaimed in the daylight. But when actions are hidden in darkness and responsibility is shared among thousands, human nature tends to let others carry the burden.'

Akbar decided to put his subjects to the test. He ordered an enormous stone reservoir built in the center of the palace square. A royal proclamation was read in every bazaar:

'By order of the Emperor, tonight between dusk and dawn, each family in Agra must send one person to pour exactly one brass cup of fresh cow's milk into the royal reservoir. The pool must be filled under cover of night, without lanterns, as a quiet offering of loyalty!'

Throughout the night, thousands of citizens filed into the dark square, stepped to the stone rim of the reservoir, tipped their vessels, and hurried home.

Every single citizen reasoned identically: 'There are forty thousand families in Agra pouring rich, foaming milk into this giant pool. If I pour one cup of plain water instead of milk, no one will notice in the pitch dark, and my water will be swallowed up by the ocean of white milk!'

At sunrise, Emperor Akbar walked proudly to the square with Birbal, expecting to behold a magnificent white lake of sweet milk.

Instead, Akbar gasped in horror. The reservoir was filled to the brim with crystal-clear, transparent water! Not a single citizen had brought milk; every single household had brought water!

Birbal smiled: 'Behold, Your Majesty. When responsibility is diffused and darkness conceals the act, everyone assumes someone else will do the right thing. True virtue is what a man does when he knows no one will ever find out.'

Akbar laughed at the humbling revelation, thanked Birbal for the lesson, and resolved to build civic integrity through education rather than blind decree.
